questions.stem: A histogram class 20 < x ≤ 30 has frequency density 1.5 and class width 10. What is the frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency = frequency density x class width = 1.5 x 10 = 15. In a histogram, frequency is represented by the AREA of the bar, not its height. A very common error is reading the height as the frequency.

questions.stem: Data is grouped with unequal class widths: 0-10 (freq 20), 10-30 (freq 60), 30-50 (freq 40). What are the frequency densities?
questions.explanation: Frequency density = frequency / class width. For 0-10: 20/10 = 2. For 10-30: 60/20 = 3. For 30-50: 40/20 = 2. Option (b) gives the frequencies, not frequency densities.

questions.stem: A histogram bar for the class 5 < t ≤ 15 has height 4 (frequency density). The bar for 15 < t ≤ 20 has height 6. How many more data values are in the second class than the first?
questions.explanation: Class 5-15: freq = 4 x 10 = 40. Class 15-20: freq = 6 x 5 = 30. Difference = 30 - 40 = -10, so the second class has 10 fewer values. Despite the taller bar, the narrower width means fewer data values. This is why histograms use frequency density for the y-axis.

questions.stem: A histogram has total area of 120 (representing 120 data values). The bar for 0 < x ≤ 5 has area 30. What proportion of data values fall in this class?
questions.explanation: Proportion = area of bar / total area = 30/120 = 1/4 = 25%. In a histogram, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency, so the proportion of data in a class equals the proportion of total area.

questions.stem: A histogram shows: 0-5 (freq density 3), 5-10 (freq density 5), 10-20 (freq density 2), 20-40 (freq density 1). What is the total frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency = FD x width for each class. 0-5: 3x5=15. 5-10: 5x5=25. 10-20: 2x10=20. 20-40: 1x20=20. Total = 15+25+20+20 = 80. You must multiply each frequency density by its own class width.
